analysis.one_liner: Lets gun violence victims sue gun makers and sellers by repealing the industry's legal immunity.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in a House Judiciary subcommittee after being referred on the day it was introduced.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 2005, a federal law has blocked most lawsuits against firearm and ammunition makers, dealers, and their trade association when a gun is criminally misused, even by someone else. This bill would repeal that shield so victims of gun violence could sue the industry in state or federal court like victims of any other product. It would also unlock ATF's gun-trace database so crime-gun trace data could be used as evidence in civil cases. The bill was sent to the House Judiciary Committee and its Constitution subcommittee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Victims of gun violence and their families, who would regain the right to sue manufacturers, dealers, and sellers for negligent or unlawful practices — such as supplying guns to traffickers — the same way people can sue makers of other dangerous products. State and local governments and the public would also gain from the industry facing normal legal accountability for how its products reach the illegal market.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gun violence victims and their families

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals sections 2 through 4 of the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act, the 2005 law that prohibits civil actions against firearm and ammunition manufacturers, sellers, importers, dealers, and trade associations for criminal misuse of a firearm by a third party [S2] [S3].

With the shield gone, victims of gun violence could bring negligence and other civil claims in state or federal court, including cases based on how a dealer sold or supplied a gun that was later used in a crime [S2].

The bill makes the ATF Firearms Trace System database subject to subpoena and admissible as evidence, so plaintiffs could use federal crime-gun tracing data in court instead of being barred from it [S2] [S3].
It would also allow administrative proceedings against industry members for unlawful conduct, not just private lawsuits [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers, dealers, importers, sellers, and their trade association, which would lose the broad civil liability immunity they have held since 2005 and face ordinary litigation costs, judgments, and insurance expenses.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun manufacturers, dealers, and trade associations

drawbacks.text: Repealing the shield exposes lawful manufacturers and dealers to lawsuits over criminal acts by third parties they did not control, and industry backers argue that is unfair liability for products that are legal to sell and can be misused by others [S2].
Litigation costs, judgments, and insurance premiums would be passed into gun prices and could push smaller dealers out of business, costs that fall partly on law-abiding gun buyers.

Opening the ATF trace database to discovery puts a sensitive law-enforcement database containing ongoing investigation data into general civil litigation, which law-enforcement agencies have traditionally resisted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: victims gain ordinary access to the courts, and the gun industry loses a liability shield no other industry enjoys. The strongest objection — that makers of a legal product should not answer for criminal misuse by strangers — is precisely what the 2005 law answered by statute; this bill would return the industry to the same rules every other manufacturer lives under, decided case by case by courts rather than by blanket immunity.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, then sent to its Constitution and Civil Justice subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Adam Schiff introduced the bill on February 1, 2016, with 35 original cosponsors, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1] [S3] [S5].
Four weeks later, on February 29, 2016, it was referred to the Subcommittee on the Constitution and Civil Justice, the last action of its life [S5].
The bill ended the 114th Congress with no committee vote and no House floor vote, a routine path for legislation a committee majority declines to act on [S5].
All 60 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearm manufacturers, dealers, and their trade association kept the 2005 civil liability shield intact, and their exposure to gun violence lawsuits ended when the Congress did.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun manufacturers kept their liability shield

industries.industry: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers, dealers, and their trade association
industries.note: The bill would have repealed the PLCAA shield that has protected the industry from most civil lawsuits over criminal misuse of its products since 2005, and would have made federal gun-trace data usable as evidence against it. Because the bill died, the industry's immunity and the information shield both remain in place.
Repealing the immunity would have created a new field of civil cases for lawyers representing gun violence victims, with fees contingent on winning for their clients.
